_about: TRAINING examples for the intent classifier. Day 14b.
THIS FILE IS THE TRAIN SPLIT AND NOTHING ELSE. The test split is the `routing`
array in tool_cases.json, which was written on Day 14 — before any classifier
existed — and is not edited to make these numbers look better. It contains a case
labelled `known_miss` precisely because the keyword router cannot catch it, so the
held-out set is hostile to the incumbent rather than to the challenger.
benchmarks/23_intent_classifier.py asserts the two files are DISJOINT by message
text. A classifier evaluated on its own training data reports its memory, not its
accuracy, and that assertion is what stops this file drifting into the test set.
WHY LABELLED EXAMPLES AND NOT KEYWORDS. A keyword router matches the strings
someone thought of. 'can you note down that the ADBMS sheet needs updating' needs
'note down' to be in a list; 'could you jot down' needs 'jot down' added, and so
on without end. These examples are not matched against the message — they are
embedded into the same 384-dimensional space the retriever already uses, and the
message is classified by where it LANDS in that space. Phrasings nobody wrote
down still land near the ones that are.
THE `none` CLASS IS THE LARGEST ON PURPOSE. A false positive puts a decision in
front of a human that should never have been raised; a miss merely does nothing.
Many of the `none` examples deliberately reuse task vocabulary inside questions,
because that is the error that costs something.
